strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: avoiding negative transfer from unreliable teachers, including teachers that perform worse than independently trained students.

The classification method is simple and compatible with multiple distillation losses. Tables 1, 2, and 4 report improvements across several teacher–student architectures, with some students exceeding the from-scratch baseline despite substantial teacher underperformance.
Experiments span classification, gridworld reinforcement learning, and steering prediction. The RL evaluation includes 10 random seeds and comparisons with SAC and IBRL.
weaknesses: The steering experiment has a fundamental methodological inconsistency. Appendix A.5.1 specifies residual-based conformal intervals using a single calibration quantile. With the stated absolute-residual score, C(x) = [fT(x) − q, fT(x) + q], so its length is always 2q. Consequently, thresholding interval length produces a constant weight rather than sample-dependent guidance. No input-dependent scale or alternative interval construction is described, leaving the claimed adaptive mechanism and Table 3 gains unexplained.

The RL coverage claim is unsupported. Calibration uses teacher-generated trajectories, whereas student training changes the state distribution and updates the student policy online. Exchangeability and independence conditions are not established. Moreover, covering actions sampled from the teacher does not establish that those actions are correct or useful under domain shift.

Conformal marginal coverage does not guarantee that singleton sets identify accurate teachers or that set size reliably ranks teacher usefulness. Appendix A.2 gives gradient identities and a pointwise MSE interpolation, but does not establish improved generalization or transfer. Empirical coverage, teacher error conditional on set size, and retained-guidance rates are missing.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of conformal prediction. Missing controls include maximum-probability or entropy gating, random gating matched to the retained fraction, and tuned reductions of the fixed distillation coefficient. These are particularly important because classification AUKT simply disables guidance for non-singleton sets. Positioning against existing adaptive or confidence-weighted distillation is also insufficient.

The RL implementation is unclear: Section 3.3.2 proposes uncertainty-weighted KL regularization, while Section 4.2 describes action selection plus an exploration schedule. It is unspecified whether both mechanisms are used, how student recalibration works, and whether baselines receive the same schedule. The observed gains therefore cannot be confidently attributed to the proposed uncertainty mechanism.

Evaluation breadth exceeds its depth. Classification uses only CIFAR-100 with two Gaussian-noise settings; driving uses one offline steering dataset with synthetic noise. Classification and steering results lack repeated-run variability, despite several small gains. There are no substantive sensitivity studies for calibration size, coverage level, or gating choices.

Calibration independence is problematic in the driving protocol: Appendix A.5.2 trains the teacher on the full training partition before selecting calibration examples from that same partition. This does not provide the independent held-out calibration data required by the stated split-conformal argument.

Several reported deltas are incorrect. In Table 2, FitNet for WRN-40-2→WRN-16-2 improves from 70.15 to 71.26, which is 1.11 rather than 0.11; PKT for ResNet110→ResNet20 improves from 66.58 to 67.58, which is 1.00 rather than 0.20. These errors warrant a numerical audit.

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: transferring useful knowledge from teachers that become unreliable under distribution shift.
The proposed gating mechanism is simple and compatible with multiple distillation losses and teacher–student architectures.

Reports consistent improvements over the corresponding ungated baselines across classification, gridworld RL, and steering prediction. The RL experiments include 10 random seeds, and several classification results exceed training the student from scratch.
weaknesses: The driving formulation has a major unresolved technical problem. Appendix A.5.1 uses residual-based conformal intervals with a single calibration quantile. Under the stated absolute-residual construction, every interval has width 2q, so the uncertainty and binary guidance weight are constant across inputs. This cannot implement the claimed sample-adaptive guidance without an additional, unspecified mechanism, leaving Table 3 insufficiently explained.

The RL coverage claim is unsupported. Calibration uses teacher-generated trajectories, whereas student training changes the state distribution and policy over time; exchangeability is not established. Moreover, covering actions sampled from the teacher does not establish that those actions are correct or useful, especially under domain shift.

Conformal marginal coverage does not establish that singleton sets identify reliable teacher predictions or that larger sets identify harmful guidance. No selective-error analysis or empirical coverage measurements validate this central connection. The generic quantile definition also omits the finite-sample correction needed for the stated exact coverage guarantee.

The experiments do not isolate the value of conformal prediction. Missing comparisons include confidence or entropy gating, random gating at a matched retention rate, and tuning the overall distillation weight. Without these controls, the gains could result primarily from reducing harmful teacher supervision. The related-work discussion also insufficiently positions the contribution against adaptive and uncertainty-aware distillation.

Appendix A.2 provides algebraic observations about weighted losses rather than a performance guarantee. It assumes uncertainty identifies erroneous guidance and does not establish improved generalization. Its description of conventional distillation as enforcing strict teacher adherence is misleading because the baseline also includes ground-truth supervision.

Evaluation breadth exceeds evaluation depth: classification uses only CIFAR-100 with two Gaussian-noise configurations, RL uses three small gridworlds, and driving measures offline steering accuracy. Classification and driving lack seed counts and uncertainty estimates; sensitivity to calibration size, coverage level, and gating choices is untested. Several reported gains are too small to assess reliably without repeated runs.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. The driving calibration split is taken after teacher training on the parent training set, compromising standard held-out calibration assumptions. The online student calibration procedure and the relationship between RL loss weighting and action selection are underspecified. Table 2 also contains incorrect deltas: 71.26−70.15 is 1.11, not 0.11, and 67.58−66.58 is 1.00, not 0.20.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical problem: transferring useful knowledge from teachers whose predictions become unreliable under distribution shifts, including teachers that underperform students trained from scratch.

The classification mechanism is simple and compatible with several distillation objectives. Tables 1, 2, and 4 report consistent improvements across multiple teacher–student architectures, with some improvements exceeding one percentage point.
The evaluation spans classification, imitation-guided reinforcement learning, and steering prediction. The RL experiments use ten random seeds and show promising learning-efficiency gains.
weaknesses: The regression construction has a fundamental problem. With the absolute-residual score specified in Sections 3.3.1 and A.5.1, a single calibration quantile produces C(x) = [f_T(x) − q, f_T(x) + q], whose length is always 2q. Consequently, thresholding interval length gives the same guidance weight for every input, rather than adaptive guidance. The reported steering improvements therefore cannot be attributed to the stated sample-dependent mechanism without an additional, undocumented construction.

Conformal coverage does not establish the reliability of the selected teacher guidance. Marginal coverage does not guarantee low error conditional on obtaining a singleton set, nor that set size reliably orders teacher errors. Appendix A.2 differentiates the weighted objective and gives a pointwise MSE solution, but does not prove improved generalization or establish the necessary relationship between uncertainty and harmful guidance.

The RL conformal justification is incomplete. Calibration actions come from teacher rollouts, so coverage concerns teacher-generated actions rather than optimal or successful actions. Correlated trajectories, changing student visitation distributions, and online student updates also require justification beyond ordinary split conformal prediction. Additionally, Section 3.3.2 describes uncertainty-weighted KL regularization, whereas Section 4.2 emphasizes action selection; their precise relationship in the implementation is unclear.

The comparisons do not isolate the benefit of conformal prediction. Missing controls include entropy or maximum-probability gating, random gating at the same selection rate, and tuning a smaller constant distillation weight. There are no substantive ablations of calibration size, coverage level, selection threshold, or the RL exploration schedule. Comparisons with existing adaptive or uncertainty-aware distillation approaches are also needed to establish novelty beyond confidence-based filtering.

The breadth of applications exceeds the depth of validation. Classification uses only CIFAR-100 with two Gaussian-noise settings, RL uses small fully observable gridworlds, and driving evaluates offline steering accuracy on one dataset. Classification and driving results lack seed variability or confidence intervals, despite many classification gains being small. Empirical coverage and the relationship between prediction-set size and teacher correctness are not reported.

Reporting and reproducibility need improvement. RAPS configuration and online RL calibration details are insufficiently specified, and the driving threshold selection is ambiguous. Several reported deltas are incorrect: in Table 2, FitNet for WRN-40-2 to WRN-16-2 improves from 70.15 to 71.26, which is 1.11 rather than 0.11; PKT for ResNet110 to ResNet20 improves from 66.58 to 67.58, which is 1.00 rather than 0.20. Claims of surpassing scratch training also need qualification because some AUKT configurations remain below that baseline.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: exploiting useful guidance without inheriting errors from unreliable teachers or pseudo-labels. The proposed prediction-set-size weighting is simple and readily integrated into existing objectives.

The empirical study spans knowledge distillation, semi-supervised classification, gridworld reinforcement learning, and steering prediction, with generally positive reported results across multiple architectures and guidance methods.

Classification experiments include four-run means and standard deviations, while gridworld experiments use ten seeds. Hyperparameter sensitivity studies, hard-weighting variants, and computational overhead measurements provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The steering experiment has a fundamental methodological inconsistency. Appendix A.6.1 uses residual-based split conformal prediction with a single global quantile. Under the absolute-residual construction in Section 3.1, prediction intervals have constant width 2q, so interval-size uncertainty and its thresholded weight cannot vary across inputs. No locally adaptive scale or alternative construction is specified. Consequently, the described method cannot support the claimed sample-adaptive mechanism behind Table 3.

The conformal justification exceeds what the procedures establish. Marginal coverage does not make prediction-set size a calibrated measure of individual guidance reliability. SSL explicitly reuses labeled training examples for calibration, violating the independence required by standard split CP. RL uses dependent policy rollouts and changing state distributions. Moreover, Section 3.1 omits the finite-sample corrected quantile needed for its stated coverage guarantee. Appendix A.7 acknowledges using CP heuristically, but this does not resolve the stronger claims elsewhere.

RL calibration uses actions generated by the imitation policy itself, rather than labels establishing action quality. This can measure policy concentration without detecting confidently bad actions under shift. The paper provides no convincing measurement linking its uncertainty estimates to guidance errors or action value.

The RL implementation and proposed objective are insufficiently reconciled. Section 3.2.3 specifies uncertainty-weighted KL regularization, whereas the experiments describe uncertainty-based action selection with an additional annealing schedule that increasingly forces RL actions. Ablations separating these components, including matched schedules for baselines, are needed to attribute the gains to conformal weighting.

The distillation comparisons do not isolate adaptive weighting from simply reducing harmful teacher influence. There is no tuned fixed-weight or mean-weight-matched control. Large headline improvements mainly repair severely degraded vanilla KD: for ResNet110 to ResNet20, KD rises from 57.23% to 66.53%, essentially matching the 66.51% scratch student. Other configurations show useful gains, but the strongest headline numbers overstate evidence for extracting additional teacher knowledge.

Evaluation breadth is stronger than evaluation depth. Distillation and driving shifts are limited to fixed Gaussian corruptions, and RL uses three small gridworlds. SSL uses a shortened 51,200-iteration budget without showing whether gains persist at convergence or comparing against stronger adaptive pseudo-label weighting methods. Driving results lack variability estimates.

Important implementation details remain unresolved, including RAPS settings, online RL calibration data and refresh procedures, and handling empty classification prediction sets. With the stated SSL score, empty sets are possible; the proposed normalization then yields negative uncertainty and weights above one, contradicting the claimed range. These gaps, together with the unresolved soundness concerns, make the paper insufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: exploiting imperfect teachers or pseudo-labels without allowing unreliable guidance to dominate learning. The proposed weighting mechanism is simple and readily integrates with existing objectives.

The empirical study spans knowledge distillation, semi-supervised classification, gridworld navigation, and steering prediction. Tables 1–4 report improvements across multiple architectures and learning methods, with four repeated runs for classification and ten seeds for gridworld experiments.

The appendix includes hyperparameter sensitivity, alternative weighting functions, training details, and computational overhead measurements. Table 6 reports only a small training-time increase over standard knowledge distillation.
weaknesses: The steering implementation does not explain how guidance can be sample-adaptive. Appendix A.6.1 uses residual-based split conformal prediction with a single calibrated quantile. Under the absolute-residual construction described in Section 3.1, the prediction interval is [f(x)−q, f(x)+q], whose width is the constant 2q. Consequently, thresholding its size produces a constant guidance weight, not sample-specific uncertainty. No locally scaled residual or other input-dependent interval construction is specified. This undermines the explanation of Table 3 and requires clarification or corrected experiments.

The claimed principled uncertainty estimates exceed what conformal prediction establishes. Marginal coverage does not guarantee that prediction-set size identifies incorrect guidance or beneficial guidance gradients. Moreover, Section 3.2.2 reuses labeled training data for calibration of the same evolving SSL model, which does not satisfy ordinary split-conformal independence. RL calibration uses dependent policy rollouts and changing state distributions; covering actions sampled from an imitation policy also does not establish their quality. Appendix A.7 acknowledges that strict coverage is not the goal, but the paper still needs evidence connecting its uncertainty scores to guidance reliability.

The experiments do not isolate adaptive selection from simply weakening harmful guidance. A tuned constant guidance coefficient, a constant weight matched to the proposed method’s average weight, and shuffled sample weights are missing. This matters because standard KD is substantially worse than training from scratch: in Table 1, the advertised 10.89-point improvement yields 70.29% accuracy versus 70.34% for the scratch student. Other combinations show useful gains, but the largest headline improvements primarily recover a degraded baseline.

The RL method and evaluation are insufficiently specified. Section 3.2.3 defines a weighted KL guidance loss, whereas Section 4.3 describes uncertainty-based action selection; their relationship in the implemented algorithm is unclear. Appendix A.5 additionally introduces an increasing probability of bypassing imitation guidance, without an ablation establishing its contribution or a clear statement that baselines receive the same schedule. The three small gridworlds therefore provide limited evidence for attributing the gains specifically to conformal guidance.

The conceptual novelty is modest relative to the broad claims: the method combines existing conformal prediction sets with conventional uncertainty-dependent weighting. Appendix A.2 explains weighted-loss behavior but does not establish an advantage specific to conformal prediction. The claim to be the first framework embedding split conformal prediction into training requires substantially stronger positioning against prior conformal training and pseudo-labeling methods.

Evaluation breadth is stronger than evaluation depth. Supervised distribution shifts are limited to selected Gaussian-noise corruptions, SSL lacks direct uncertainty-weighting comparisons, and steering results omit variability across runs. Empirical coverage and guidance-error-versus-weight analyses are absent. Important implementation details, including SSL recalibration frequency, handling empty prediction sets, and heuristic-baseline weighting and tuning, are also insufficiently documented.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: retaining beneficial teacher or expert guidance while reducing the influence of unreliable predictions. The proposed weighting mechanism is simple and easy to integrate.

The evaluation spans knowledge distillation, semi-supervised classification, gridworld navigation, and steering prediction. Classification experiments include multiple architectures and four runs; navigation experiments use ten seeds.

Reported improvements are broadly consistent across guidance methods. Hyperparameter sensitivity studies, heterogeneous teacher–student experiments, hard-weighting variants, and runtime measurements provide useful supporting evidence.
weaknesses: The steering implementation has a fundamental unresolved issue. Appendix A.6.1 uses residual-based split conformal prediction with a single calibration quantile. For the absolute-residual score described in Section 3.1, the interval is [prediction − q, prediction + q], whose width is always 2q. Consequently, thresholding interval size produces a constant weight, not input-adaptive guidance. No normalized residual score or other construction explaining variable widths is specified, undermining the interpretation of Table 3.

The conformal justification does not establish reliable guidance uncertainty in the proposed training settings. SSL reuses the labeled training data for calibration, violating the usual held-out requirement. RL uses temporally dependent policy rollouts and changing state distributions; actions sampled from the imitation policy do not establish whether its guidance is correct or valuable. Appendix A.7 acknowledges using CP heuristically, but this leaves the stronger claims of rigorous uncertainty unsupported. Marginal coverage also does not guarantee that set size ranks individual prediction errors reliably.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of conformal adaptation from simply reducing guidance strength. In Table 1, vanilla KD performs dramatically worse than training from scratch, while KD + AdaConG largely recovers scratch performance and sometimes remains below it. A tuned constant guidance coefficient, matched-average weighting, and equally tuned entropy/MSP weighting are needed to establish the source of improvement. The claim that KD + AdaConG outperforms uncertainty-aware baselines is also not uniformly supported by the table.

The RL method is inconsistent across its description and evaluation: Section 3.2.3 proposes weighting a KL guidance loss, whereas Section 4.3 and Appendix A.5 describe selecting between IL and RL actions. The additional schedule that progressively forces RL actions is not separately ablated or clearly matched across baselines, confounding attribution of the navigation gains.

Evaluation breadth exceeds its depth. Distribution shifts are largely synthetic Gaussian corruption, navigation uses three small fully observable grids, and steering reports no variability. SSL uses 51,200 training iterations without demonstrating that the gains persist for converged baselines. Calibration-set sizes and refresh procedures, baseline uncertainty-to-weight mappings, and validation procedures for hyperparameter selection are insufficiently specified.

The methodological novelty is modest: established conformal prediction sets are mapped through a monotone function to weight an existing loss or select actions. The intuitive analysis explains weighting but does not establish when set size identifies harmful guidance or improves learning. Given the unresolved implementation and evaluation issues, the evidence does not support the claimed universal framework at a top-tier acceptance standard.
